content.author: kate-waddams
content.description: Tastes, character, disease risk, distant origins: our DNA says a great deal about us. But a predisposition has never been a destiny.

hero.hook: Your DNA tells where you come from, what you like and what threatens you, but it does not decide everything.

blocks.text: Our DNA tells us a great deal about ourselves: where we came from, what our bodies can do, and possibly even what lies ahead. It is our story and our blueprint. But what exactly is it? DNA is found in almost every cell of the body. Coiled into a **double helix**, it carries the genetic instructions that govern how we function, grow, develop and reproduce.

Its strands are made of just **four small units**, the nucleotides, written A, T, C and G. The order of those four letters forms our [[genome]], a genetic blueprint unique to each of us. So what can you actually read in it? Your tastes, your disease risks, your origins. And how far does this text write your future?

A [[gene]] is a piece of that text. It works like a biological instruction sheet: it tells the body how to make its **proteins**, which in turn build and run our cells. That is where our visible traits come from. But genes play a role that goes much deeper than looks.

blocks.caption: "The Travelling Companions", by Augustus Egg (1862): two young women alike in everything, one asleep, the other reading.

blocks.text: A [[genetic variant]] is a slightly different version of a gene. Recently, scientists have linked several of them to **personality**. Subtle genetic tweaks can steer our preferences: loving exercise or hating it, being an extrovert, collecting hobbies. Our DNA may weigh on our everyday lives far more than we imagine. That raises a question: how much of our behavior is already written in our biology?
Tea or coffee? Even that simple preference may come down to subtle variations in our genes, according to the research linking DNA to personality.

And that may not be all. DNA also offers clues about who carries a [[genetic predisposition]] to certain **mental health** disorders, such as depression. So it does not only tell us what we like, but also what may make us vulnerable.

sections.title: Your genes shape your tastes and character

blocks.text: Mental health is not the only area concerned. Our DNA makeup can make us more prone to other diseases too, some of which "run in the family." A well-known example: inherited variants of the [[BRCA1 and BRCA2]] genes predispose some women to **early-onset breast cancer**.

blocks.caption: A sequencing chromatogram: each colored peak is one letter of DNA. This is the readout on which a test spots a variant.

blocks.text: This is where [[genetic testing]] earns its value, for the health system and for the people concerned. Spotting an inherited risk makes early action possible: earlier **screening**, closer monitoring, medication or other preventive treatment. That head start can save lives and reduce medical costs.

sections.title: What DNA reveals about disease risk

blocks.text: Our DNA is passed down through the generations. It keeps clues about our ancestors: where they came from, what they ate, how they lived. It is a living time machine. By comparing the **genetic patterns** of present-day populations, scientists have been able to map the route humans took across the globe.

blocks.caption: The earliest Homo sapiens lineages in Africa and their exit toward Eurasia, as reconstructed by population genetics.

blocks.text: One example. Written history tells us that people moved from **North Africa** into the [[Iberian Peninsula]] between **700 and 1200 AD**. DNA backs up the written account: people living in the peninsula today still carry the genetic traces of those encounters.

Even our deepest origins are more complicated than a simple family tree. One study using full genome sequences found evidence that two ancient human populations, which had split around **1.5 million years** ago, later mixed again.

sections.title: A time machine: where do you come from?

blocks.text: So your DNA influences many of your characteristics. But being predisposed to something does not mean your fate is sealed. Carrying a genetic risk of **depression** does not mean you will go on to develop depression. Genetic risk is not the same as certainty.

Genes open up possibilities; they do not impose them. Our experiences, our choices and our circumstances matter just as much. Reading your DNA means reading one part of yourself: a precious part, sometimes decisive for your health, but only a part.
DNA tells the story of our tastes, our risks and our origins, but a predisposition is never a certainty: your DNA is only part of you.

sources.text: Yale School of Medicine, « How Genes Shape Personality Traits: New Links Are Discovered », Yale Medicine News, 9 septembre 2024.

Institute of Medicine (US), « Genetics and Health », dans L. M. Hernandez et D. G. Blazer (dir.), Genes, Behavior, and the Social Environment: Moving Beyond the Nature/Nurture Debate, National Academies Press, Washington (DC), 2006.
NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Centre, « International study reveals how our genes shape blood proteins linked to disease ».
« What Our DNA Can Tell Us About the History of Humans », Frontiers for Young Minds, 2020.
« How genetics determine our life choices », BBC Future, 9 mai 2023.
University of Cambridge, « Genetic study reveals hidden chapter in human evolution », Research news, 18 mars 2025.

content.subtitle: Genes and fate
content.title: What can you actually learn from your DNA?

BRCA1 and BRCA2.explanation: Two genes whose inherited variants predispose some women to early-onset breast cancer. Spotting them with a test makes earlier screening, closer monitoring or preventive treatment possible.

Iberian Peninsula.explanation: The large peninsula in the southwest of Europe, today Spain and Portugal. Its present-day inhabitants still carry genetic traces of the people who came from North Africa between 700 and 1200 AD, just as written history recounts.

gene.explanation: A segment of DNA that carries the instruction for making a protein, which in turn builds and runs our cells. Our visible traits come from genes, and recent research links some of them to personality.

genetic predisposition.explanation: Carrying genes that raise the probability of developing a trait or a disease, without making it certain. A genetic risk of depression, for instance, does not mean you will suffer from it.

genetic testing.explanation: The analysis of a person's DNA in search of variants linked to a disease risk. It makes early action possible, through earlier screening or preventive treatment, which can save lives and reduce medical costs.

genetic variant.explanation: A slightly different version of the same gene, inherited from our parents, which sets individuals apart from one another. Some variants weigh on our preferences, others raise the risk of a disease such as breast cancer.

genome.explanation: The complete DNA of a person, written as a sequence of the four nucleotides A, T, C and G. It is this unique genetic blueprint that we "read" in search of tastes, disease risks and origins.
